chapter: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
title: Hearing Rene, Buddy Petit and Armstrong as a kid; Armstrong's generosity
summary: He tells of Rene against Armstrong, the Armstrong band's high Cs, and Armstrong buying him shoes.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Did you know him down here?
But you never heard him play then?

I saw him and heard him play when I was a kid. I didn't know who he was, because I wasn't interested. All I cared during that time was to dance and follow the band. That's all I cared. You didn't know the names, man. No, I didn't know the names. I heard Buddy. Player Buddy was just starting out. The first time I heard Armstrong, the dedication of the Tonlefong Playground, they had a little band to come out and play. And they had a fellow named Frazier playing the baritone. I know two or three guys. Rene was back there with him too.
Do you think Rene was like a good reader and all that too? I don't think so. His band was just ad libbing when you heard him.

Well, that's all the whole band was doing. Yeah, they weren't using music at all. Yeah, that's all they was doing. And Lee Collins told me a tale about Rene. He says one day, they were advertising the band, and he saw Louie and Louie came on and got on the wagon. He said, dude, those days it was a wagon. And they always carried a thick rope or chain. See those guys, people would take them lock the wagons together with these chains. And they couldn't get away. They just had to take it if it was better than you, see. And so they saw Rene about two blocks away with his band. And so Rene at the same time saw Lee. But Louie was hiding down in the truck, in the wagon, see. And so they came together and he gave Louie his horn and they had quite a battle there. Rene was small but he was stout. He played a lot upstairs you know. But he wasn't as strong as Louie Armstrong. He wasn't as strong as Louie Armstrong, but he was strong, much stronger than Buddy Petit. Now Buddy Petit played a whole lot of pretty stuff down in the low range. And so Louie and I were with him, we started making the 300 high Cs and in the Tiger rag, you know, in the every morning high F. We played in New York and we broke it up. We played in Boston against Fletcher Anderson, the band. And after he did that, that was it. 300, we counted. And so many courses, Tiger rag and like that. They had a lip. Yeah, oh yeah. He just batted his lip up. He had a lot of trouble. Louie had a lot of trouble, period. Here we had, he used to come out, you wouldn't let him come around until 6 o'clock. And I never saw so many cousins in my whole life. And they'd have a line about from here to, oh, longer from here to in front of his house. On both sides, he'd come out. He'd get well first to first meet. He never refused. Just like I have a, I intend to bring it, I had a right up in the Times. Sometimes you could hold my picture. Louie's a little inset right on the side. And I stated that I was with Louie Armstrong and how he fed and put shoes on my feet, which he did. During the operation after Louie disbanded his band, I was selling ads for the union. There was a little kid he called Lil Jon, a great little drummer. And something was wrong with his spine, so he was giving this benefit for his medical bills, you know. And so I met Louie and I was in bad shape. One of my shoes, the sole was loose, you know, I had it tied with a string. Every time I walked, go flip. Well I had my daughter and my mother take it, see what I'm talking about? So every time I walked, flip flop, flip flop, flip flop. So I had a string tied around. So I met him 39 South Park. He said, hey Nosey. I said, hey Dip. So he came, I said Dip, take one of these ads for me. He's taking a $20 ad and he gave me $20. Well that's the type of fellow he was. That's the type of fellow he was. So I spoke about it.
